CONSTITUTIONAL LAW  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 1
Nature and Salient Features
Short Revision Note

The Constitution establishes public institutions, distributes power and sets enforceable limits on its exercise. India combines a federal distribution of legislative powers with a strong Union. Parliamentary government, judicial review, fundamental rights, Directive Principles and an independent judiciary are core features. Recall the institutional sequence: allocate power, limit power, review its exercise.
Detailed Study Note

The Constitution is a written, supreme legal instrument. It establishes a parliamentary executive with collective responsibility to the elected House under Articles 75(3) and 164(2). The President and Governors ordinarily act on ministerial advice within the constitutional scheme. The Constitution also combines representative democracy and universal adult suffrage with protections for people and minorities.

Federalism. Articles 245–246 and the Seventh Schedule distribute legislative subjects among Union, State and Concurrent Lists. The Union’s residuary power (Article 248, subject to Article 246A), emergency powers and Parliament’s power to reorganise States illustrate centralising features. Cooperative federalism describes how both levels can work together within their assigned powers. It does not itself transfer legislative competence.

Amendment and review. Article 368 provides special procedures, including State ratification for specified changes. Some changes, such as those contemplated by Article 4, can be made by ordinary legislation. In Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) 4 SCC 225, a challenge arising from land reform broadened into a review of Parliament’s amending power. The Court held that Parliament can amend the Constitution subject to the basic structure limitation. In S.R. Bommai v Union of India, (1994) 3 SCC 1, challenges to Article 356 proclamations established that such proclamations are reviewable and affirmed federalism and secularism as basic features.

Hypothetical illustration. A State law deals with a State List subject. Start by testing legislative competence and then ask whether a fundamental right or other constitutional limitation is infringed. Those are distinct questions.
Kesavananda Bharati  |  Supreme Court judgment
Exam Practice
3 marks. Name two features that strengthen the Union.
11 marks. Discuss the salient features of the Indian Constitution and assess its federal character.
Answer plan. Define constitutional supremacy, group the features, explain federal and centralising elements, apply Kesavananda and Bommai, then conclude.
Self-test. What protects the Constitution’s basic structure against amendment?
Answer. Judicial review under the basic structure doctrine.
CONSTITUTIONAL LAW  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 2
The Preamble
Short Revision Note

The Preamble identifies the people as the source of constitutional authority and sets out the character and aims of the Republic. Remember justice, liberty, equality and fraternity. It guides interpretation and forms part of the Constitution. A legal claim must be tied to an operative constitutional provision.
Detailed Study Note

The opening words identify the authority through which the Constitution was adopted. Sovereignty concerns independent constitutional authority. Democracy concerns political power exercised through the people and representative institutions. A republic has a non-hereditary head of State. Secularism concerns the State’s relationship with religion and constitutional equal treatment. The socialist objective reflects a commitment to social and economic justice within the constitutional scheme.

The four objectives. Justice has social, economic and political dimensions. Liberty protects space for thought, expression, belief, faith and worship. Equality concerns status and opportunity. Fraternity promotes individual dignity and national unity and integrity. The Forty-second Amendment added the words Socialist and Secular and added integrity to the reference to national unity.

Case development. In Re Berubari Union, AIR 1960 SC 845, the Court described the Preamble as an aid to interpretation and took the view that it was outside the Constitution. In Kesavananda Bharati, (1973) 4 SCC 225, the Court recognised it as part of the Constitution. Its values help identify basic features and inform interpretation. Amendment remains subject to basic structure review.

Hypothetical illustration. A provision has two plausible readings. A court can consider which better respects dignity and equality within the text. A person seeking relief should identify the enforceable right or duty involved in the dispute.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Identify the four preambular objectives.
11 marks. Explain the constitutional significance of the Preamble and discuss whether it can be amended.
Answer plan. Explain source and objectives, identify the Forty-second Amendment, trace Berubari and Kesavananda and explain the interpretive role.
Self-test. Can the Preamble independently give a government authority a power?
Answer. An operative constitutional or statutory provision must confer the power.
CONSTITUTIONAL LAW  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 3
The Union and Its Territory
Short Revision Note

Articles 1–4 describe India’s territory and Parliament’s powers of territorial change. Article 2 deals with admission or establishment of new States. Article 3 deals with reorganisation, including boundary and name changes. For a proposal affecting a State’s area, boundaries or name, the President refers the proposal to its legislature for views before introduction.
Detailed Study Note

Under Article 1, India is a Union of States. The territory of India comprises the territories of States, the Union Territories in the First Schedule and territories that may be acquired. Article 2 empowers Parliament to admit or establish new States on appropriate terms and conditions.

Article 3 enables Parliament to form a new State, increase or diminish a State’s area, alter its boundaries or change its name. The Bill requires the President’s recommendation. The proviso requires a reference to the affected State legislature where applicable. Parliament must respect the consultation procedure. The State legislature’s views are consultative. The constitutional provision makes special distinctions concerning Union Territories.

Article 4 permits related changes to the First and Fourth Schedules and supplemental, incidental and consequential provisions. A law under Articles 2 or 3 is not treated as an Article 368 amendment. In Re Berubari Union, AIR 1960 SC 845, a proposal to transfer Indian territory to Pakistan raised a different issue. Cession required a constitutional amendment.

Hypothetical illustration. Parliament proposes renaming a State. Identify Article 3, require the President’s recommendation and the reference for views, then explain Parliament’s legislative role even if the State opposes the proposal.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Does an Article 3 Bill require the State legislature’s consent?
11 marks. Explain Articles 1–4 and distinguish internal reorganisation from cession of territory.
Answer plan. Define territory, distinguish Articles 2 and 3, list procedure, explain Article 4 and cite Berubari.
Self-test. Which two Schedules can be amended by an Article 4 law?
Answer. The First and Fourth Schedules.
CONSTITUTIONAL LAW  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 4
Citizenship
Short Revision Note

Articles 5–11 primarily deal with citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution and Parliament’s continuing power to legislate. The Citizenship Act, 1955 establishes acquisition by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory. Overseas Citizen of India status is a statutory form of registration with specified benefits.
Detailed Study Note

Articles 5–8 distinguish domicile and specified birth, parentage or residence conditions, migration from Pakistan, migration to Pakistan and registration of persons of Indian origin abroad. Article 9 concerns voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship. Article 10 continues citizenship subject to law. Article 11 preserves Parliament’s legislative power.

The Act. Sections 3–7 cover birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory. For birth in India, section 3 uses three periods. From 26 January 1950 to before 1 July 1987, birth generally suffices. From 1 July 1987 to before 3 December 2004, at least one parent must be a citizen. From 3 December 2004, both parents must be citizens, or one must be a citizen and the other must not be an illegal migrant at the time. Statutory exceptions apply. Section 4 has separate conditions for birth abroad. Section 6B creates a specific registration or naturalisation route linked to the statutory conditions introduced by the 2019 amendment.

Loss and OCI. Sections 8–10 address renunciation, termination and deprivation. Sections 7A–7D govern Overseas Citizen of India cardholder registration, specified benefits and cancellation or renunciation. OCI status does not grant Indian citizenship or voting rights. In In Re Section 6A of the Citizenship Act, 1955, 2024 INSC 789, the Supreme Court majority upheld the constitutionality of Assam’s special citizenship provision.
Hypothetical illustration. A child was born in India in 2007. Identify section 3 and apply the post-3 December 2004 parental conditions to the facts.
In Re Section 6A  |  Supreme Court judgment
Exam Practice
3 marks. Explain Overseas Citizen of India status.
11 marks. Define citizenship and discuss the modes of acquisition under Indian law.
Answer plan. Separate commencement provisions from the Act, list statutory methods, explain the birth dates, and add loss and OCI.
Self-test. Which Article empowers Parliament to legislate on citizenship?
Answer. Article 11.
CONSTITUTIONAL LAW  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 5
State under Article 12
Short Revision Note

Article 12 identifies the State for Part III. It includes the Union and State governments and legislatures, local authorities, and other authorities within India or under the control of the Government of India. For a society or corporation, examine whether it is financially, functionally and administratively dominated by government.
Detailed Study Note

Why it matters. Identifying the respondent under Article 12 helps determine whether a Part III right directed against the State can be enforced. A municipality is the familiar local authority. A registered society or company can be an instrumentality where the evidence establishes the required degree of governmental domination.

The test. Ajay Hasia v Khalid Mujib Sehravardi, (1981) 1 SCC 722, concerned admissions by an engineering college run by a society. The Court examined practical indicia including funding, monopoly, public functions and government control. Pradeep Kumar Biswas v Indian Institute of Chemical Biology, (2002) 5 SCC 111, held CSIR to be State on cumulative evidence of financial, functional and administrative domination particular to the body and pervasive in character. General regulatory control alone is insufficient.

The boundary. Zee Telefilms Ltd v Union of India, (2005) 4 SCC 649, held by majority that BCCI was outside Article 12 on the record before the Court. Article 226 can still reach a private body in relation to an enforceable public duty. For the judiciary, distinguish administrative action from judicial orders. A judicial order of a superior court is ordinarily challenged through the applicable judicial remedies, as illustrated by Naresh Shridhar Mirajkar, AIR 1967 SC 1.
Hypothetical illustration. A society receives a grant. Ask who appoints its board, directs its decisions and finances its operations. Receiving a grant is one fact in the overall inquiry.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Name the bodies expressly included in Article 12.
11 marks. Explain other authorities under Article 12 with leading cases.
Answer plan. Set out the text, explain the instrumentality test, apply Ajay Hasia and Pradeep Kumar Biswas, and distinguish public-duty review under Article 226.
Self-test. Does general statutory regulation make a body State?
Answer. General regulation alone is insufficient.
CONSTITUTIONAL LAW  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 6
Availability of Fundamental Rights
Short Revision Note

Ask three questions for any Part III problem. Who holds the right? Against whom is it enforceable? What remedy fits? Articles 14, 20 and 21 use person-based language. Article 19 protects citizens. Articles 15, 16 and 29 also use specific citizenship language. Some rights reach private conduct.
Detailed Study Note

Persons and citizens. Article 14 protects any person within India, and Articles 20 and 21 protect persons. Article 19 freedoms belong to citizens. Article 15(1) and Article 16 concern citizens, while Article 29(1) protects any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture. Article 29(2) protects citizens in the specified admission context. Article 30 is framed around religious and linguistic minorities.

State and private conduct. Many rights operate against State action. Articles 15(2), 17, 23 and 24 can reach specified private conduct. Article 15(2) concerns access and use in the circumstances and on the grounds stated in the text. Article 23 addresses trafficking and forced labour, including by private persons. Article 24 has an age and work-category threshold.

Companies and citizenship. State Trading Corporation v Commercial Tax Officer, AIR 1963 SC 1811, held that a company is not itself a citizen for Article 19. Bennett Coleman & Co v Union of India, (1972) 2 SCC 788, examined newsprint controls affecting newspapers and recognised that citizens’ speech rights could be affected through the corporate medium. Identify whose right is asserted.

Hypothetical illustration. A private shop refuses entry solely on caste grounds. Identify the citizen and the private respondent, then examine Article 15(2) and the specific place, ground and disadvantage covered.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Give two rights available to persons and two constitutional provisions framed for citizens.
11 marks. Discuss who may claim Fundamental Rights and against whom they may be enforced.
Answer plan. Group citizen and person rights, explain Article 12 and horizontal examples, and add the company and shareholder distinction.
Self-test. May a non-citizen invoke Article 21?
Answer. Yes. Article 21 protects persons.
CONSTITUTIONAL LAW  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 7
Judicial Review under Article 13
Short Revision Note

Article 13 makes laws inconsistent with Part III void to the extent of inconsistency. Clause (1) deals with pre-Constitution laws and clause (2) restrains the State from making rights-infringing laws. Severability can preserve unaffected parts. Eclipse describes how an inconsistent pre-Constitution rule may be inoperative in the relevant field while the constitutional shadow remains.
Detailed Study Note

Scope. Article 13(3) includes ordinances, orders, rules, regulations, notifications, bye-laws and customs or usages having the force of law. Judicial review asks whether the law exceeds legislative competence or violates the Constitution. Article 13 is central for rights review, while jurisdiction and remedies often arise under Articles 32 and 226.

Doctrines. Under severability, ask whether the remainder can operate independently and whether the legislature can reasonably be taken to have intended it to survive. R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla v Union of India, AIR 1957 SC 628, illustrates the severability inquiry. Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v State of Madhya Pradesh, AIR 1955 SC 781, applied eclipse to a pre-Constitution law whose operative conflict was later removed by constitutional amendment. Basheshar Nath v CIT, AIR 1959 SC 149, illustrates the restriction on waiver of fundamental rights, particularly equality protection.

Constitutional amendments. Article 13(4) excludes amendments under Article 368 from Article 13. Kesavananda Bharati subjects constitutional amendments to a separate basic structure limit. Identify whether the instrument is ordinary law, delegated legislation or a constitutional amendment before selecting the test.

Hypothetical illustration. A statute has an independent licensing chapter and an unconstitutional censorship clause. Ask whether the licensing regime can function by itself and whether it would have been enacted independently.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Explain the doctrine of eclipse.
11 marks. Discuss Article 13 as a mechanism for judicial review of legislation.
Answer plan. Compare clauses (1) and (2), define law, apply severability, eclipse and waiver, and distinguish basic structure review.
Self-test. Does one invalid clause automatically invalidate the entire Act?
Answer. Apply severability to determine what can survive.
CONSTITUTIONAL LAW  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 8
Right to Equality
Short Revision Note

Articles 14–18 protect equality through different rules. Article 14 prohibits arbitrary State action and allows reasonable classification. Article 15 addresses specified discrimination and enables special provisions. Article 16 concerns public employment. Article 17 abolishes untouchability, and Article 18 regulates titles.
Detailed Study Note

Article 14. A classification needs an intelligible differentia separating the groups and a rational nexus between that differentia and the law’s objective. In Ram Krishna Dalmia v Justice S.R. Tendolkar, AIR 1958 SC 538, the Court articulated principles of reasonable classification. In E.P. Royappa v State of Tamil Nadu, (1974) 4 SCC 3, a civil service dispute gave rise to the formulation linking equality and arbitrariness.

Articles 15 and 16. Article 15(1) bars discrimination against citizens on specified grounds. Article 15(2) reaches specified access restrictions. Clauses (3)–(6) enable defined special provisions, including for women and children, disadvantaged groups and economically weaker sections. Article 16(1)–(2) protects equality of opportunity in State employment. Distinguish the enabling provisions in clauses (4), (4A), (4B) and (6). Indra Sawhney v Union of India, 1992 Supp (3) SCC 217, addressed OBC reservation, creamy layer and the general 50 per cent rule in its context. Janhit Abhiyan v Union of India, (2023) 5 SCC 1, upheld the 103rd Amendment providing for EWS reservation.

Articles 17 and 18. Article 17 makes enforcement of disabilities arising from untouchability punishable according to law. Article 18 bars State titles other than military or academic distinctions and regulates acceptance of foreign titles and benefits. Balaji Raghavan v Union of India, (1996) 1 SCC 361, distinguished national awards from titles when used consistently with constitutional limits.

Hypothetical illustration. A scholarship is restricted to applicants below an income threshold. Identify the objective, ask whether income is a meaningful distinction and explain how it relates to the purpose of the scheme.
Exam Practice
3 marks. State the two tests of reasonable classification.
11 marks. Explain the right to equality under Articles 14–18, with cases and examples of substantive equality.
Answer plan. Start with Article 14, distinguish Articles 15 and 16, explain enabling provisions, and give short notes on Articles 17 and 18.
Self-test. Which provision specifically governs equality of opportunity in public employment?
Answer. Article 16.
CONSTITUTIONAL LAW  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 9
Right to Freedom
Short Revision Note

Article 19 protects six citizen freedoms. Articles 20 and 21 protect persons against specified criminal and liberty violations. Article 21A guarantees free and compulsory education for ages six to fourteen. Article 22 distinguishes ordinary arrest from preventive detention. Match each interference to the particular Article and its legal test.
Detailed Study Note

Article 19. The freedoms are speech and expression, peaceful unarmed assembly, association including unions or cooperative societies, movement, residence and occupation or trade. Clauses (2)–(6) tailor restrictions to the particular freedom. For speech, Article 19(2) lists sovereignty and integrity, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation and incitement to an offence. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Court struck down section 66A of the IT Act for unconstitutional restrictions on speech.

Articles 20, 21 and 21A. Article 20 covers retrospective criminal liability or enhanced punishment, prosecution and punishment twice for the same offence, and compelled self-incrimination by an accused. Maneka Gandhi v Union of India, (1978) 1 SCC 248, arose from passport impounding and held that procedure affecting liberty must meet fairness requirements. Articles 14, 19 and 21 may operate together. K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India, (2017) 10 SCC 1, unanimously recognised privacy as a fundamental right. Under Article 359, a Presidential order suspending the right to move courts for enforcement of specified Part III rights cannot include Articles 20 or 21.

Article 22. In ordinary arrest, clauses (1)–(2) protect information about grounds, access to legal counsel and production before a magistrate within 24 hours excluding journey time. Clause (3) excepts enemy aliens and preventive detention from these two clauses. Clauses (4)–(7) provide a separate regime including limits linked to Advisory Board review, communication of grounds and an early opportunity to make a representation, subject to stated exceptions.
Hypothetical illustration. A public authority bars online criticism using a vague rule. Identify Article 19(1)(a), test the claimed Article 19(2) ground and examine how the rule is drawn and applied.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Can enforcement of Article 21 be suspended by an Article 359 order?
11 marks. Explain Articles 19–22 with particular reference to personal liberty and safeguards against arrest.
Answer plan. Group freedoms and specific grounds, explain Article 20 protections, apply Maneka Gandhi, and distinguish the two Article 22 regimes.
Self-test. Which provision protects an accused against compelled self-incrimination?
Answer. Article 20(3).
Unit I Revision Checklist
Recall. Federal features and basic structure • Articles 1–4 and 5–11 • Articles 12 and 13 • Tests under Articles 14, 19, 21 and 22.
CONSTITUTIONAL LAW  /  UNIT II  /  TOPIC 1
Right Against Exploitation
Short Revision Note

Article 23 prohibits trafficking in human beings, begar and similar forms of forced labour. It reaches private and State conduct. Article 24 prohibits employment of children below fourteen in factories, mines or other hazardous employment. The two provisions protect against different kinds of exploitation.
Detailed Study Note

Forced labour. Begar refers to compulsory labour typically exacted without payment. Article 23 has broader reach. Coercion may be physical, legal or economic. Clause (2) allows compulsory service for public purposes and prohibits discrimination in imposing it on grounds only of religion, race, caste or class.

In People’s Union for Democratic Rights v Union of India, (1982) 3 SCC 235, workers engaged on Asian Games construction projects received less than the minimum wage. The Supreme Court treated labour for less than the minimum wage in those circumstances as forced labour under Article 23. Bandhua Mukti Morcha v Union of India, (1984) 3 SCC 161, concerned quarry workers and illustrates the State’s obligations to identify, release and rehabilitate bonded labourers under the applicable framework.

Child employment. Article 24 states the constitutional minimum protection for children below fourteen in the specified work. The Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986, as amended, has a wider statutory framework with defined exceptions and distinct rules for adolescents.

Hypothetical illustration. A contractor pays workers below the statutory minimum and claims they chose to accept the amount. Examine the employment conditions and apply the Article 23 reasoning in PUDR.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Define begar.
11 marks. Explain the scope of Articles 23 and 24 with reference to forced labour and child labour.
Answer plan. Define exploitation, explain Article 23 and its exception, apply PUDR, then distinguish Article 24 and statutory protection.
Self-test. Can Article 23 reach a private contractor?
Answer. Yes. Its prohibition extends to specified private conduct.
CONSTITUTIONAL LAW  /  UNIT II  /  TOPIC 2
Freedom of Religion
Short Revision Note

Articles 25–28 protect conscience, religious practice and denominational affairs while allowing specified regulation. Article 25 is an individual right. Article 26 concerns denominations. Article 27 addresses taxes specifically appropriated to promote or maintain a particular religion. Article 28 regulates religious instruction and worship in educational institutions.
Detailed Study Note

Article 25 protects freedom of conscience and the right of all persons freely to profess, practise and propagate religion, subject to public order, morality, health and other Part III provisions. Clause (2) preserves regulation of secular activities associated with religion and legislation for social welfare or reform, including opening Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus.

Article 26 protects religious denominations and their sections, subject to public order, morality and health. It covers institutions, managing affairs in matters of religion, owning and acquiring property, and administering property in accordance with law. Shirur Mutt, AIR 1954 SC 282, distinguished matters of religion from secular administration. In Bijoe Emmanuel v State of Kerala, (1986) 3 SCC 615, the Court protected pupils who respectfully stood during the national anthem but declined to sing for reasons of conscience.

Articles 27 and 28. Article 27 concerns taxes whose proceeds are specifically appropriated to promote or maintain a particular religion or denomination. Article 28(1) bars religious instruction in wholly State-funded institutions, subject to the endowment or trust exception in clause (2). In recognised or aided institutions, clause (3) guards against compelled participation without the prescribed consent.

Hypothetical illustration. A school receiving State aid requires a student to attend religious worship. Examine Article 28(3), the student’s consent or guardian’s consent where the student is a minor, and the relevant facts.
Exam Practice
3 marks. List the limits expressly applicable to Article 25(1).
11 marks. Discuss the scope and limits of religious freedom under Articles 25–28.
Answer plan. Distinguish individual and denominational rights, explain secular regulation, and finish with taxes, instruction and consent.
Self-test. Which provision protects a denomination’s management of its affairs in matters of religion?
Answer. Article 26(b).
CONSTITUTIONAL LAW  /  UNIT II  /  TOPIC 3
Saving of Certain Laws
Short Revision Note

Articles 31A, 31B and 31C create different protections. Article 31A covers specified categories and generally protects against Articles 14 and 19. Article 31B concerns Ninth Schedule enactments, subject to basic structure review of post-24 April 1973 insertions. Article 31C protects laws genuinely implementing Article 39(b) or (c) against Articles 14 and 19.
Detailed Study Note

Article 31A. The five categories concern estates and related rights, limited takeover of property management, corporate amalgamation, specified corporate management or shareholder rights, and specified mineral agreements or interests. A State law requires presidential assent following reservation for consideration. The text also contains a compensation safeguard for specified personally cultivated land within the ceiling and associated structures.

Article 31B protects the listed Acts and Regulations against Part III objections within its terms. In I.R. Coelho v State of Tamil Nadu, (2007) 2 SCC 1, the Court held that constitutional amendments inserting laws into the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are reviewable where the impact on protected rights damages the basic structure. An exam answer should distinguish the ordinary law and the constitutional amendment inserting it.

Article 31C. Kesavananda Bharati upheld the protection for laws implementing Article 39(b) or (c) while rejecting the exclusion of judicial scrutiny of the asserted nexus. Minerva Mills v Union of India, (1980) 3 SCC 625, invalidated the Forty-second Amendment’s expansion to all Directive Principles. Property Owners Association v State of Maharashtra, 2024 INSC 835, confirmed that the earlier protection survives and that privately owned resources may qualify under Article 39(b) depending on their character and context.

Hypothetical illustration. A statute declares that it implements Article 39(b) and claims immunity. Identify the rights invoked and examine whether the statutory provisions genuinely serve the directive. The declaration alone cannot settle the question.
Property Owners Association  |  Supreme Court judgment
Exam Practice
3 marks. What is the significance of 24 April 1973 for the Ninth Schedule?
11 marks. Compare Articles 31A, 31B and 31C and explain their limits.
Answer plan. Compare subject matter, protection and review, then use Coelho and Property Owners Association to explain the current position.
Self-test. Does Article 31C protect every law implementing any Directive Principle?
Answer. Its surviving protection is confined to laws giving effect to Article 39(b) or (c).
CONSTITUTIONAL LAW  /  UNIT II  /  TOPIC 4
Cultural and Educational Rights
Short Revision Note

Article 29(1) protects any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture. Article 29(2) protects citizens from admission denial on specified grounds only in State-maintained or State-aided institutions. Article 30 protects religious and linguistic minorities in establishing and administering educational institutions of their choice.
Detailed Study Note

Article 29. Conservation of language, script or culture is protected under clause (1). Its wording extends to any qualifying section of citizens. Clause (2) addresses denial of admission on grounds only of religion, race, caste, language or any of them. It specifies the institutions to which it applies.

Article 30. Clause (1) protects establishment and administration. Clause (1A) safeguards the right when property of a minority institution is compulsorily acquired. Clause (2) bars discrimination in granting aid on the ground that an institution is under minority management. Minority status in the educational context is generally assessed State-wise under T.M.A. Pai Foundation v State of Karnataka, (2002) 8 SCC 481.

Permissible regulation. In T.M.A. Pai the Supreme Court distinguished institutional autonomy from the State’s power to prescribe legitimate educational standards. Read the scope of regulation with reference to the institution’s type and whether it receives aid. St. Xavier’s College v State of Gujarat, (1974) 1 SCC 717, illustrates that standards and measures against maladministration may be permissible while control destroying protected autonomy raises constitutional problems.

Hypothetical illustration. A State requires teaching qualifications at a minority college and also proposes to take over all management appointments. Examine each requirement separately for its purpose, reach and effect on administration.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Who can invoke Article 29(1)?
11 marks. Discuss cultural and educational rights and explain the limits of regulation of minority institutions.
Answer plan. Separate the clauses of Article 29, explain Article 30, and use T.M.A. Pai to analyse permissible standards and autonomy.
Self-test. Is Article 29(1) confined to religious and linguistic minorities?
Answer. It protects any qualifying section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture.
CONSTITUTIONAL LAW  /  UNIT II  /  TOPIC 5
Directive Principles of State Policy
Short Revision Note

Articles 36–51 guide governance and lawmaking. Article 37 makes them non-enforceable by courts and fundamental in governance. In an exam, group them by purpose and explain how they interact with enforceable Part III rights.
Detailed Study Note

Structure. Article 36 adopts the Part III meaning of State unless the context otherwise requires. Articles 38 and 39 concern social order and policy aims such as livelihood, distribution of material resources and prevention of concentration of wealth. Article 39A concerns equal justice and free legal aid. Article 40 concerns village panchayats. Articles 41–43B cover matters such as assistance within State capacity, humane work conditions, maternity relief, living wages, worker participation and cooperative societies.

Other directives. Article 44 concerns a uniform civil code. Article 45 addresses early childhood care and education below six years, while Article 21A lies in Part III. Articles 46–48A concern weaker sections, public health, agriculture and animal husbandry, and environmental protection. Articles 49–51 address monuments, separation of judiciary from executive in public services and international peace. Socialist, Gandhian and liberal-intellectual groupings are teaching categories whose boundaries can overlap.

Part III and Part IV. State of Madras v Champakam Dorairajan, AIR 1951 SC 226, held that the admissions arrangement could not be sustained by invoking a Directive Principle against an enforceable right. Minerva Mills v Union of India, (1980) 3 SCC 625, held that harmony and balance between Parts III and IV form part of the basic structure. Article 31C provides limited protection in the Article 39(b) and (c) context.

Hypothetical illustration. A legal aid scheme gives practical effect to Article 39A. The Directive Principle explains the policy objective. Authority for specific eligibility and remedies must be located in the applicable legal framework.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Explain the effect of Article 37.
11 marks. Explain the importance of the Directive Principles and their relationship with Fundamental Rights.
Answer plan. Define their status, group key Articles, trace Champakam and Minerva Mills, and connect them to governance.
Self-test. Which Directive Principle concerns free legal aid?
Answer. Article 39A.
CONSTITUTIONAL LAW  /  UNIT II  /  TOPIC 6
Fundamental Duties
Short Revision Note

Article 51A contains eleven duties of citizens. Ten were added by the Forty-second Amendment in 1976. The Eighty-sixth Amendment added the duty of a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to a child or ward aged six to fourteen.
Detailed Study Note

A recall grouping. Clauses (a)–(d) concern constitutional and national obligations: respect the Constitution and its institutions, National Flag and National Anthem, cherish the ideals of the freedom struggle, uphold sovereignty, unity and integrity, and defend and render national service when called upon.

Clauses (e)–(h) concern harmony, dignity of women, heritage, environment and inquiry. Promote harmony across diversities and renounce practices derogatory to women’s dignity. Preserve the heritage of composite culture. Protect the natural environment and have compassion for living creatures. Develop scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform.

Clauses (i)–(k) concern public property and renouncing violence, striving for excellence, and education opportunities for children aged six to fourteen. Duties can inform interpretation and support valid implementing laws. In AIIMS Students’ Union v AIIMS, (2002) 1 SCC 428, a challenge involving institutional preference led the Court to discuss the interpretive relevance of duties, including excellence. Any sanction must have a valid legal basis.
Hypothetical illustration. A person damages a public bus. Article 51A(i) identifies the civic duty. Any criminal or civil consequence depends on the applicable law and proof of its elements.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Explain two Fundamental Duties.
11 marks. Discuss the origin, content, importance and enforcement of Fundamental Duties.
Answer plan. State the amendments, group the clauses, explain legislative implementation and give an example.
Self-test. What age group does Article 51A(k) cover?
Answer. Six to fourteen years.
CONSTITUTIONAL LAW  /  UNIT II  /  TOPIC 7
Union Judiciary
Short Revision Note

Articles 124–147 govern the Supreme Court. Revise composition, appointments, independence and routes to jurisdiction. Article 131 concerns specified federal disputes, Articles 132–136 appeals and special leave, Article 137 review, Article 143 advisory references and Article 32 enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
Detailed Study Note

Composition and independence. Article 124 provides for the Chief Justice of India and other judges, with their number determined by parliamentary law. Judges are appointed by the President and retire at 65. Article 124(4) prescribes removal for proved misbehaviour or incapacity after an address by each House supported by a majority of its total membership and at least two-thirds of members present and voting, in the same session.

Appointments. Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v Union of India, (1993) 4 SCC 441, established judicial primacy through a collective process. In Re Special Reference No. 1 of 1998, (1998) 7 SCC 739, clarified collegium consultation. In the NJAC case, Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v Union of India, (2016) 5 SCC 1, the Court invalidated the Ninety-ninth Amendment and NJAC Act, restoring the collegium framework. The constitutional appointing authority remains the President.

Powers. The Court is a court of record with contempt power (Article 129). It has specified original, appellate, review, advisory and writ jurisdiction. Article 136 special leave is discretionary. Article 141 makes its declarations of law binding on all courts in India. Article 142 enables orders necessary for complete justice in a cause or matter before it.

Hypothetical illustration. A private litigant wants to appeal directly to the Supreme Court from a tribunal. Ask whether a statutory appeal exists. A request for special leave under Article 136 invokes discretion and is subject to its constitutional limits.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Distinguish review under Article 137 from advisory jurisdiction under Article 143.
11 marks. Discuss the composition, independence and jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.
Answer plan. Explain appointment, tenure and removal, group the jurisdiction Articles, and mention Articles 141 and 142.
Self-test. Which Article governs specified federal disputes in the Supreme Court’s original jurisdiction?
Answer. Article 131.
CONSTITUTIONAL LAW  /  UNIT II  /  TOPIC 8
State Judiciary
Short Revision Note

Articles 214–231 cover High Courts. Revise composition, appointment and removal, Article 226 writs, Article 227 superintendence and Article 215 court-of-record powers. Articles 233–237 deal with subordinate courts, including High Court control under Article 235.
Detailed Study Note

Composition and appointment. Article 214 provides for High Courts for States and Article 231 permits a common High Court. Article 216 provides for a Chief Justice and other judges. Under Article 217 the President appoints after the constitutionally specified consultation, operating through the judicially developed collegium framework. A High Court judge retires at 62. Article 217 refers to the procedure in Article 124(4) for removal. Transfer is addressed in Article 222.

Jurisdiction. Article 225 preserves jurisdiction subject to the Constitution and competent law. High Courts exercise civil and criminal appellate jurisdiction in accordance with applicable enactments and original jurisdiction where conferred. Article 226 authorises writs for Fundamental Rights and for other purposes within its scope. Article 227 gives superintendence over courts and tribunals in the territory, subject to the armed forces exception. Article 215 provides court-of-record status and contempt power.

Subordinate courts and review. Article 233 concerns district judges and Article 235 places control over subordinate courts with the High Court. L. Chandra Kumar v Union of India, (1997) 3 SCC 261, arose from tribunal jurisdiction and affirmed constitutional judicial review under Articles 226 and 227 and Article 32 as part of the basic structure.

Hypothetical illustration. A statutory tribunal gives a decision and the litigant alleges a jurisdictional error. Check statutory remedies and identify the distinct functions of writ review and superintendence.
Exam Practice
3 marks. How is a High Court judge appointed?
11 marks. Explain the composition, jurisdiction and powers of High Courts.
Answer plan. Set out Articles 214, 216 and 217, explain tenure and removal, distinguish Articles 226 and 227, and mention Article 235.
Self-test. What is the ordinary retirement age of a High Court judge?
Answer. Sixty-two years.
CONSTITUTIONAL LAW  /  UNIT II  /  TOPIC 9
Writ Jurisdiction and Judicial Activism
Short Revision Note

Article 32 guarantees access to the Supreme Court for Part III enforcement. Article 226 also reaches other enforceable legal rights and public duties. Recall the five writs by function: release, compel, stop, quash and test title to public office.
Detailed Study Note

Five writs. Habeas corpus tests detention and can secure release from unlawful custody. Mandamus compels performance of an enforceable public duty. Prohibition restrains proceedings in excess of jurisdiction. Certiorari can quash a decision affected by jurisdictional error or another recognised review ground. Quo warranto tests legal entitlement to hold a substantive public office. The right, respondent, stage and relief govern the choice.

Articles 32 and 226. Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right and is tied to Part III. Article 226 extends to other public law grounds, subject to territorial jurisdiction and discretionary principles. Under Article 226(2), cause of action arising wholly or partly within the territory can support jurisdiction. An ordinary alternative remedy may weigh against writ relief. Whirlpool Corporation v Registrar of Trade Marks, (1998) 8 SCC 1, identifies recognised exceptions including lack of jurisdiction, denial of natural justice and enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

Judicial activism and PIL. Public interest litigation can relax standing where affected groups face barriers to access. Andi Mukta v V.R. Rudani, (1989) 2 SCC 691, allowed mandamus against an aided college trust in relation to a public duty. Vishaka v State of Rajasthan, (1997) 6 SCC 241, issued workplace harassment guidelines in a legislative gap. It is a historical example, now to be read with the 2013 statute on workplace sexual harassment. Judicial remedies remain constrained by constitutional competence and applicable law.

Hypothetical illustration. A public authority refuses to perform a clear statutory duty owed to an applicant. Identify the duty and right, check alternative remedies and consider mandamus under Article 226.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Distinguish prohibition and certiorari.
11 marks. Compare Articles 32 and 226, explain the five writs and assess the role of PIL.
Answer plan. Compare scope, territory and remedies. Explain each writ in one sentence, then illustrate public duty and PIL with cases.
Self-test. Which writ tests a person’s legal title to a substantive public office?
Answer. Quo warranto.
